items.title: Nordwand Mono – A monospace font for coders and adventurers
items.content:
A compact neo-grotesk font designed for coding.

I'm very passionate about the font I am using for my terminal and overall neovim experience, and I couldn't find the "perfect" font. So I decided to design one from scratch using python. This font aims to bring some elements from the all time classic "Univers" font into the proportions of the "JetBrains Mono" font. The name "Nordwand" is a reference to switzerland and its iconic typography – bringing it into the stiff and cold atmosphere of the swiss north faces.

Amongst the inspirations for the design, you might identify:

Some alternative character designs are available to tweak the vibe of the font to your liking. See the alternative characters document for a visual comparison and the corresponding OpenType feature tags.

Only two minimal ligatures are exposed with "->" and "=>". I might add a full set of ligatures later on, but I personally won't be using them.

This font is generated with python. Each glyph is drawn from a python glyph class, in which you can inject a drawing context object. You can for example modify some metrics like the x-height, the capital height etc.

To do so, override the config.example.yml with the values of your liking. Be sure to visualize the individual glyphs with python -m visualize --config config.yml <glyph_id> . Then you can geneate the full font with python -m generate_font --config config.yml . The font files will be generated inside ./custom-fonts .

There are no guarantees that the font might look good with different metrics, and some glyphs might require some tweaking if the metrics are altered !

items.title: The Netherlands is building its own Linux OS to break free from Microsoft
items.content:
Serving tech enthusiasts for over 25 years.

TechSpot means tech analysis and advice you can trust .

Microsoft No More: European countries are increasing efforts to build sovereign digital infrastructure to replace Microsoft and other US-based solutions. The Dutch government is even working on its own Linux distribution because The Hague is reportedly tired of Washington's threats against EU-based institutions.

The Dutch government is trying to solve its digital sovereignty problem with its own Linux operating system. A local source recently highlighted the development efforts being poured into NixOS , a Linux distro that originated as a package manager created by Dutch developers. The idea is that US-based software solutions, most notably Microsoft's, would eventually be replaced by this new OS and open-source productivity solutions.

Nix is a package manager with a few peculiar features, including cross-platform compatibility and its own functional programming language for configuring Unix and Unix-like systems. The tool was first released in 2003, and NixOS debuted three years later. The Linux distro is built around Nix and is currently supported by the Dutch nonprofit organization NixOS Foundation.

Nix and NixOS are the foundations of the Digitaal Autonome Werkomgeving Overheid (DAWO) project, which includes all the tools required to build a sovereign IT infrastructure. With DAWO, The Hague plans to provide government and public institutions with a custom operating system, productivity and office applications, cloud services, management tools, and everything in between .

Serious efforts to build the DAWO-based sovereign infrastructure apparently began a few months ago, when Dutch authorities decided to standardize the creation of a national IT ecosystem. The project is focused on accessibility, because NixOS developers are not exactly enthusiastic proponents of heavily GUI-based computer interfaces.

DAWO's first pilot programs have already been deployed in private and local environments, but the plan should eventually encompass all institutions in the Netherlands. Sovereignty efforts in the country apparently stalled for years, but the new US administration provided the right incentives to finally get the job done.

Mozilla is betting Europe's digital sovereignty push can help fund Firefox

Washington authorities recently decided to target the Hague-based International Criminal Court (ICC) with sanctions, while Microsoft allegedly blocked the court's prosecutors from accessing its email and other crucial IT services. The ICC is already replacing Microsoft Office with an open-source alternative, as DAWO and NixOS are going to extend the sovereignty efforts even further.

Earlier this year, the Netherlands blocked an attempt by a US company to buy a crucial app used by Dutch citizens . Elsewhere in Europe, countries are investing millions in massive conversion projects based on the same concept: replacing Windows, Microsoft, and most US software services with Linux, open-source software, or other custom solutions.

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: The US is ordering every civilian agency to rip out DeepSeek, even tools built on it
items.content:
Markwayne Mullin in his official US Senate portrait, taken before he became Homeland Security Secretary. Image: United States Senate / Wikimedia Commons, Public domain, cropped

The US government has ordered every federal civilian agency to strip DeepSeek out of its computers and stop buying it, along with any third-party product built on the Chinese lab's AI. The Department of Homeland Security filed notice of the order with the Federal Register on Monday, under a 2018 supply chain law that lets it bar risky technology from government systems.

The order, numbered 2026-01 and signed by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, is dated July 24, 2026. It was kept out of public view until this week. Its notice is due to appear in the Federal Register on Tuesday, October 20, under docket DHS-2026-0628.

The order tells all civilian agencies to do two things. First, exclude Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence, its affiliates and their products from purchasing "effective immediately", including agency-approved product lists, e-commerce marketplaces and similar buying channels. Second, remove products from DeepSeek and its affiliates, "and third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations", from agency IT systems immediately.

That second clause is the wide one. DeepSeek's models are released as open weights, so they turn up inside other companies' tools as well as in DeepSeek's own app and website. The order does not list which products it means, and it does not say how agencies should treat a DeepSeek model running on a US company's servers. It also comes days after DeepSeek updated its cheap Flash model , which it says now beats Claude Opus 5 at some coding tasks.

It does not reach the military or spy agencies. The order applies to federal civilian executive branch agencies "except for their national security systems and secure compartmented information systems", which fall under the Pentagon and the Director of National Intelligence.

The order's summary of risks says DeepSeek's servers are in China and that Chinese law "permits extensive authority to government cyber and intelligence functions to access private company infrastructure". It says DeepSeek's sign-up process collects personal information and may "track and digitally fingerprint users", and that its apps work by having people type in information, which could mean sensitive data from US government staff or contractors ends up in China.

Combined with public data, that information "could produce actionable intelligence on U.S. persons and/or government programs", the order says. It adds that the models "may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities", and cites a February 2025 NowSecure audit that found multiple critical flaws in DeepSeek's iPhone app.

The order's evidence is drawn from public material: DeepSeek's own privacy policy, a 2020 DHS business advisory on Chinese data risks and an April 2025 House Select Committee on China report. It doesn't describe any case of government data reaching DeepSeek.

Agencies that can't comply can ask for an exception, such as having the order not apply to them, to certain actions, or a delay. Requests must be made in writing within 60 days of the order's issue, with a "compelling justification", for example the impact on mission-critical work, and any alternative safeguards. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) reviews them and approves or refuses in writing.

Until DeepSeek products are gone, agencies are told to monitor traffic in and out of their networks, step up logging, add controls against data leaving their systems and flag anything unusual. CISA can help agencies that lack the skills to comply, and the Secretary must review the order within a year and every year after.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다
